challenges.title: Winter storms
challenges.sub: Extratropical cyclone tracks and central pressure
challenges.question: How far off is each model's forecast storm centre for strong winter cyclones (explosive deepening), 1-5 days ahead?
challenges.sample: 12 explosive cyclones of winter 2025-26 (6 Atlantic, 3 North Pacific, 3 North America), 46 start times; events chosen before any forecast was downloaded.
challenges.truth: No independent observed storm centre exists, so tracks are scored against two analyses: ECMWF's and NOAA GFS's.

tables.title: Track error, km (mean of 24-120 h)
tables.note: Lower is better. Ranks are 95 % ranges from resampling whole storms.

findings: Both ECMWF models beat GFS on track under either truth, including against GFS's own analysis, so this is not a home advantage.
AIFS and IFS cannot be told apart; central-pressure errors (3-5 hPa) do not separate any model.
caveats: AI models run here from the ECMWF analysis (Pangu, FuXi, FengWu, GraphCast, SFNO, Aurora) join when their runs finish.

challenges.title: Hurricane intensity
challenges.question: How well do models forecast hurricane strength (maximum wind) and rapid intensification, 1-5 days ahead?
challenges.sample: Every 2026 Atlantic, eastern and central Pacific forecast case (414 starts), the same cases as the hurricane-track test.
challenges.truth: NHC's working 2026 best tracks. About three quarters of the cases are eastern Pacific storms, whose intensities come mostly from satellite estimates (about ±10 kt).

tables.title: Late: high-resolution and hurricane-specialised models
tables.note: Mean absolute error of maximum wind, averaged over 24-120 h; lower is better. RI = rapid intensification (+30 kt in 24 h); ROC area 1.0 = perfect.

tables.title: Early: available at advisory time (fair comparison with NHC)
Global models, forecast centres' own trackers
Global models, the same tracker for all
Consensus at advisory time: our trackAI-I vs NHC (* = built after seeing 2026 results)
rows: Linear corrected consensus of trackAI-I inputs, early *
Plain average of trackAI-I inputs, early *

findings: Google DeepMind's cyclone model has the smallest intensity error of all, ahead of every physics hurricane model.
At advisory time, the HCCA consensus and NHC's official forecast lead; NHC also separates rapid-intensification cases best.
Coarse global models are much too weak (by 14-42 kt), so their tables mostly measure that weakness; ECMWF AIFS shows no rapid-intensification signal.

Our intensity consensus trackAI-I ties NHC's neural-net aids but trails HCCA and NHC official by about 3 kt in 2026 (it runs too weak); it beats every physics hurricane model when built from same-start runs.
caveats: Groups are ranked separately because they differ in timing and resolution.
AI models run here from the ECMWF analysis join the global table when their track runs finish.

challenges.title: Atmospheric rivers
challenges.sub: West Coast water-vapour transport and rain
challenges.question: How well do models forecast strong water-vapour transport (atmospheric rivers) reaching the US West Coast, 1-5 days ahead?
challenges.sample: 51 starts, November 2025 to March 2026, 67 coastal points; 114 coastal rain gauges.
challenges.truth: Water-vapour transport (IVT) from the ECMWF analysis and, separately, from the GFS analysis; daily rain at coastal gauges (independent).

tables.title: Equitable threat score (ETS) for IVT ≥ 250 kg/m/s, mean of 24-120 h
tables.note: Higher is better (1 = perfect, 0 = no skill).

findings: The order is the same under either analysis, and AIFS also leads on observed coastal rain.
caveats: The ECMWF analysis favours ECMWF models and models started from it; the GFS analysis favours GFS.
Six AI models run here from the ECMWF analysis join when their runs finish.

challenges.title: Heavy rain
challenges.sub: Rain above NOAA Atlas 14 return amounts
challenges.question: Can models forecast rain heavy enough to exceed the local 2-year 24-hour amount (NOAA Atlas 14), days 1-3?
challenges.sample: 38 starts, July-October 2026 (every 3rd day), every 0.1° land cell with Atlas 14 values, area-weighted.
challenges.truth: MRMS radar-gauge rain analysis; NOAA Stage IV as an independent check gives the same picture.

tables.title: As run: ETS at the 2-year amount, days 1-3
tables.note: Frequency bias = forecast events / observed events (1 = right number).

tables.title: Same distribution correction for every model
tables.note: Each model's rain amounts mapped to the observed distribution, the same way for all.

findings: No clear winner as run: every model's rank range spans many places.
AI models almost never produce 2-year amounts (8-14 % as many events as observed); with the same correction for all they reach about the level of the best models.
caveats: † version chosen using this test period (no re-tuning since).
No model hit a single 100-year amount.

challenges.title: Heat and hard freeze
challenges.question: How well do models forecast extreme heat (above each station's own 95th-percentile maximum) and hard freeze, days 1-3?

tables.title: ETS by event (mean of days 1-3)
tables.note: Higher is better. – = the model lacks a variable the event needs (e.g. humidity for the heat index).

findings: rainfallAI-T and NOAA's NBM lead; both are corrected with observations.
Among raw models, Aurora 1.5, AIFS and FuXi lead; GraphCast and WeatherNext 2 run too cool on hot days.
caveats: A freeze forward test (new forecasts only) ranks after 7 complete cycles.

challenges.title: Air quality
challenges.question: How well does NOAA's air-quality model forecast daily ozone and PM2.5 at monitors, compared with simple baselines?
challenges.sample: July-October 2026, 12 UTC forecasts, about 1,200 EPA AirNow monitors; EPA's daily definitions.
findings: The model beats both simple baselines for both pollutants; its bias-corrected version is best.
Wildfire-smoke days make the PM2.5 ranges wide.
caveats: ECMWF CAMS and Microsoft's Aurora air-pollution model are being added.

challenges.title: Energy weather
challenges.question: How well do models forecast sunshine at the ground and wind at turbine height, days 1-2?
challenges.truth: NOAA SURFRAD and SOLRAD irradiance stations; radiosondes for 100 m wind (assimilated by every centre, so not fully independent).

tables.title: Solar: 6-h mean irradiance (GHI), RMSE W/m²
tables.note: 16 NOAA ground stations; lower is better.

tables.title: Hub-height (100 m) wind vs weather balloons, vector RMSE m/s (pilot, not ranked)
tables.note: 65 balloon sites at 00 and 12 UTC; 100 m wind interpolated between reported levels.

findings: AIFS is clearly first for solar on day 1; every model is too bright by 10-20 W/m².
For 100 m wind AIFS has the smallest vector error, but it is the smoothest and too slow by about 0.9 m/s; GFS has almost no speed bias.
caveats: The AI models run here do not output radiation or 100 m wind, so they are not scored.

challenges.title: Severe thunderstorms
challenges.question: Given only its own forecast fields, how well does each model pick out where severe weather (tornado, wind or hail reports) occurs?
challenges.sample: Two separate samples: July-October 2026 and spring (March-June) 2026, every 3rd day, US land cells, area-weighted.

tables.title: July-October 2026 (38 starts): ROC area
tables.note: ROC area of the same instability-and-shear index computed from every model's fields; 1.0 = perfect, 0.5 = no skill. Ensemble means are listed but not in the single-run ranking. Still running (not ranked yet): FuXi, Atlas.

findings: July-October: GraphCast and IFS share first place; GFS is last.
Spring: the three models scored so far are tied on day 1; IFS leads on day 2. AI models join when their runs finish.
SPC's forecasters are far ahead; they also see high-resolution models and observations.
caveats: The index is deliberately simple (700 hPa is the only mid-level every model stores); it measures the large-scale setup, not storms themselves.
Storm reports are denser near people, for every model alike.

rules: Each test's question, sample, truth and scores were written down before any forecast was compared with the truth; every look at the results is logged.
Every ranked model is scored on the same cases; models lacking a needed variable are listed separately, never dropped silently.
AI models we run start from the ECMWF analysis for these tests; operational products from their own analyses.
Gridded scores are area-weighted; uncertainty is shown as 95 % ranges and rank ranges from resampling independent cases.
